title: Tikka Masala Naan, Bombay Spice Chips, and Beet Tikka Patties: Indian Food Just Swept America's Top Grocery Awards
excerpt: Three Indian-inspired brands earned top honours at the 2026 NEXTY Awards — the natural food industry's equivalent of the Oscars — in a year that confirmed Indian cuisine's breakout moment in American retail.
body:
At the 2026 Natural Products Expo West in Anaheim — the largest natural food trade show on the continent — a quiet revolution played out in the awards ceremony. Three brands rooted in Indian culinary traditions took home or competed for NEXTY Awards, the natural food industry's highest recognition for innovation, integrity, and impact. Together, they told a story that the American grocery aisle has been slow to absorb: Indian food is not a niche. It is the next mainstream.

## Keya's Snacks: The Food Network Champion Who Put Bombay in a Chip Bag

The loudest splash came from Keya's Snacks, which won a coveted NEXTY Award outright — the crowning moment of a breakout week that included a featured spot at the StartUp CPG / Advantage Pitch Slam and an appearance at the exclusive Alley Rally showcase.

The brand is the creation of Keya Wingfield, a Food Network Champion who grew up in Mumbai and has lived in the United States for nearly two decades. Her kettle-cooked potato chips come in two varieties: Bombay Spice, a complex blend of 29 single-origin Indian spices including coriander, turmeric, fenugreek, and dry mango; and Black Salt, a tangy counterpart that Wingfield calls "the cultural cousin of salt and vinegar."

The chips are made with potatoes from America and organic spices sourced directly from farmer partners in northwestern India who employ local women and offer a living wage. Every bag carries the name of Wingfield's son Daksh, who passed away at two months old.

"I wanted to create a product that was half Indian and half American, much like me, much like my household," Wingfield told *The Kitchn*. "And this all fit together perfectly — my Indian American dream."

Keya's Snacks are now stocked at Publix and available through Faire for independent retailers nationwide. The Bombay Spice chips have been called "selling out" by multiple reviewers.

## Truly Indian: 150,000 Hand-Stretched Naans a Day

Truly Indian, the consumer brand of ADF Foods — a fourth-generation family company founded in India in 1932 — earned two NEXTY finalist placements: one for its Tikka Masala Naan and another for its Crispy Chili Mango Chutney.

The Tikka Masala Naan is a category first: the only frozen naan in U.S. retail that is vegan, Non-GMO Project Verified, low-glycemic, Kosher, and Halal certified simultaneously. Each naan is hand-stretched by artisans and baked in traditional clay ovens in India, then frozen and shipped — a production process that scales to approximately 150,000 naans daily without sacrificing the bubbled, charred texture that home cooks chase.

Since launching in May 2024, Truly Indian has expanded to more than 1,300 stores across natural, conventional, and club channels. The brand's lineup extends beyond naan to include frozen samosas, high-protein roti wraps (marketed as "India's answer to the burrito"), plant-based frozen entrées, and shelf-stable cooking sauces.

"Indian cuisine is now the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America," said Rasa Kumar, SVP at ADF Foods. The NEXTY recognition, he added, validates that the category is accelerating "even as many global food categories face tariff-related cost pressures and pricing volatility."

## Hey!Hunger: Tikka Meets the Veggie Burger

The third Indian-inflected brand in the NEXTY conversation was Hey!Hunger, founded by Shireen Khera in San Francisco. Her Organic Roasted Beet & Walnut Tikka Veggie Patties earned a finalist nod for their ultra-low-processed ingredient list and the distinctive umami flavour that traditional Indian spices bring to the plant-based category.

Built around roasted beets, walnuts, legumes, and digestible plant proteins, the patties contain no isolates, fillers, or artificial additives — a profile that sets them apart in a crowded freezer section still dominated by heavily processed pea-protein alternatives.

"Hey!Hunger is an ode to the food I grew up eating and the way my mother nourished our family," Khera said. "Indian cooking has always celebrated plants, spices, and balance long before 'plant-based' became a trend."

## The Bigger Picture

What makes the 2026 NEXTY sweep significant is not just the awards themselves, but what they signal about where Indian food sits in the American consumer consciousness. A decade ago, Indian cuisine in the frozen aisle meant a few dusty boxes of chicken tikka masala from brands that treated South Asian food as a subcategory of "ethnic." Today, brands founded by Indian-American entrepreneurs are winning innovation awards for products that are vegan, organic, clean-label, and culturally specific — the exact attributes that command premium shelf space.

For the 4.8 million Indian Americans in the United States, these brands represent something more personal. They are the flavours of home, packaged for the country they now call home, and finally earning the mainstream recognition that every NRI who has ever brought samosas to a potluck always knew they deserved.

## What's Next

Keya's Snacks is eyeing national distribution beyond Publix. Truly Indian is pushing deeper into club channels. And Hey!Hunger is expanding its tikka-inspired line. The common thread: none of these founders is watering down Indian flavour to appeal to an imagined American palate. They are betting — and the NEXTY judges agree — that bold, authentic Indian taste is exactly what the American grocery shopper wants next.
